newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bonn and Bundesbank dig in for EMU gold showdown.
newsitem.headline: Bonn and Bundesbank dig in for EMU gold showdown.

text.p: Germany's government and central bank dug in on Saturday for an unprecedented showdown over Bonn's surprise plan to revalue the Bundesbank's reserves to help it qualify for European monetary union (EMU).
Finance Minister Theo Waigel, under make-or-break pressure to meet the Maastricht criteria squarely, publicly lectured the proud Bundesbank about the primacy of politics in Germany.

According to Der Spiegel magazine, Bundesbank president Hans Tietmeyer has broken one of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's strictest taboos by asking whether Germany and France should consider delaying the single currency.

A Bundesbank spokesman denied Tietmeyer had suggested a delay in his last meeting with Der Spiegel, which was back in March, but did not clarify whether he might have said it since then. Spiegel said it had the story from its sources.

Grumbling within the parliamentary ranks grew as several deputies from Kohl's centre-right coalition either announced they would oppose any change in the Bundesbank law or hinted strongly that the plan as it now stands was unacceptable.

As if that were not enough, Kohl's junior coalition ally, the pro-business Free Democrats (FDP), warned his government could collapse if Waigel tried to armtwist them into agreeing to a rise in petrol taxes to help fill his budget gaps.
And the opposition Social Democrats (SPD) urged Kohl to call early elections rather than wait until late 1998.

Waigel's statement, echoed in a letter to fellow deputies by CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble, marked a new escalation in the bullion battle that broke out last Wednesday when the Bundesbank sharply rejected his revaluation plan.

"I expect the Bundesbank to respect the legislative independence of politics just as politics always respects the independence of the Bundesbank in monetary policy," Waigel told journalists in Pfaffenhausen, a southern German resort, during a bicycle tour on this holiday weekend.
Schaeuble wrote: "The decision on the question we now face is to be taken by the legislature, whose independence is not less than that of the Bundesbank."

Tietmeyer, whose clout rests in the enormous credibility his bank enjoys among stability-minded Germans, appeared to be fighting back fiercely by raising the question of an EMU delay. Bank sources have said privately in the past that delay should not be a taboo if France and Germany could not qualify for EMU.
Kohl, 67, who has opted to run for reelection one last time just to see his life dream of deeper European unity reach the EMU stage, has long warned any delay would kill the project.
"Wouldn't it be a possibility, together with France, to agree to a delay in the start of the euro?" Der Spiegel quoted Tietmeyer as saying in an article to be published on Monday.
Spiegel, citing unnamed sources, said Tietmeyer did not believe it would be wrong if currency union were delayed if Bonn and Paris did not meet the entry criteria this year.
Waigel said a delay to EMU, due to start in 1999, would only unsettle financial markets. He also said any delay must be agreed by the European Union council of ministers.
"It does not make sense to discuss a delay in currency union," Waigel told reporters.
The Maastricht Treaty has requirements on budget deficits and debts, interest rates, inflation and foreign exchange rates that must be met in 1997 to join currency union at the start.
Waigel, who has rejected loud opposition calls for his resignation was at pains to defuse the personal angle.
"I have no problems with Hans Tietmeyer," he declared.
Waigel also said he saw no opposition among CDU deputies to the gold plan, which parliament will begin debating on Thursday.

At least two coalition deputies -- one CDU and one from the allied Free Democratic Party (FDP) -- have come out against the plan. Kohl commands only five votes more than the absolute majority he needs to change the Bundesbank law in parliament.
The Bild am Sonntag newspaper reported Waigel would next week call for higher petrol taxes and a delay in reducing the solidarity tax surcharge to pay for rebuilding east Germany.
"The CDU will have to look for another coalition partner for a decision like that," FDP economic spokesman Paul Friedhoff told the Sunday newspaper.

The opposition Social Democrats (SPD) said Kohl should call a general election as his coalition was now so split over how to fill proojected shortfalls in government finances for 1997 and 1998 and meet the criteria for the single currency.

"The economic and finance policies of the Kohl government have failed. The coalition is so split it's not capable of acting. It would be good for Germany if it cleared the path for fresh elections," SPD leader Oskar Lafontaine said.
Waigel wants to use the windfall from revaluing the gold and currency reserves to retire debt. Schaeuble said this was the correct solution to Germany's budget problems.
